blocks.title: What Tor measures
blocks.body: Four sources, four pictures of the same groups.

items.label: Torsion
items.body: $\mathrm{Tor}_1(R/x,M)$ is the $x$-torsion of $M$, $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/n,A) = A[n]$ and $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},B)$ is the whole torsion subgroup; and $\mathrm{Tor}_1(A,-) = 0$ exactly for torsion-free $A$ over $\mathbb{Z}$. This is the origin of the name.

items.label: Lost injectivity
items.body: Tensoring an injection can produce a non-injective map, and Tor records the kernel: for $0\to F_1\to F_0\to A\to0$ free, $\mathrm{Tor}(A,M) = \ker(F_1\otimes M\to F_0\otimes M)$. Quick's lecture shows that multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ becomes zero after $\otimes\mathbb{Z}/2$, and defines Tor over $\mathbb{Z}$ as exactly this kind of kernel.

items.label: Derived intersection
items.body: For ideals $I,J$, $A/I\otimes A/J = A/(I+J)$ is the ring of the naive intersection; the higher $\mathrm{Tor}_i(A/I,A/J)$ correct it, and Serre's alternating sum of their lengths is the intersection multiplicity.

items.label: Balanced bifunctor
items.body: Tor is the homology of the total complex of $P_\bullet\otimes Q_\bullet$, which treats both variables alike; nLab presents Tor as the homology of the derived tensor product, and the Michigan notes use the double complex to prove the symmetry $\mathrm{Tor}_n(M,N)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n(N,M)$.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/12\oplus\mathbb{Z}/18,\ \mathbb{Z}/8\oplus\mathbb{Z})$.
2. Show that $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}(A,B)$ is a torsion group for all $A,B$ (write $A$ as a filtered colimit of finitely generated subgroups).
3. Let $R = k[x,y]$ and $I = (x)$, $J = (y)$. Compute $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(R/I,R/J)$ for all $i$, and compare with $(I\cap J)/IJ$.
4. Over $R = k[x]/(x^2)$, compute $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(k,k)$ for all $n$ and compare with the $\mathbb{Z}/4$ example.
5. Show that $\mathrm{Tor}^{\mathbb{Z}}_1(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: Ext: definition and computations
blocks.body: Ext is the right derived functor of Hom, in either variable. Where Tor records lost injectivity of $-\otimes M$, Ext records lost surjectivity of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,M)$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(M,-)$: Quick's lectures start from the map $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2)\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2)$ induced by $2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, which is zero although $2$ is injective.

blocks.title: Ext
blocks.body:
Let $A, B$ be left $R$-modules. Choose a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ and set
$$\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B) = H^n\big(\mathrm{Hom}_R(P_\bullet,B)\big) = R^n\mathrm{Hom}_R(-,B)(A),$$
the cohomology of the cochain complex $0\to\mathrm{Hom}(P_0,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(P_1,B)\to\cdots$. By the balancing theorem below, the same groups arise from an injective resolution $B\to I^\bullet$ of the second variable: $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)\cong H^n(\mathrm{Hom}_R(A,I^\bullet)) = R^n\mathrm{Hom}_R(A,-)(B)$. Thus:

1. $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(A,B) = \mathrm{Hom}_R(A,B)$, by left exactness of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$.
2. $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(P,B) = 0$ for $n>0$ if $P$ is projective, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,I) = 0$ for $n>0$ if $I$ is injective.
3. A short exact sequence $0\to A'\to A\to A''\to0$ gives a long exact sequence
$$0\to\mathrm{Hom}(A'',B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A',B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A'',B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A',B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^2(A'',B)\to\cdots$$
and a short exact sequence $0\to B'\to B\to B''\to0$ gives
$$0\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B')\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B'')\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B')\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to\cdots.$$
The first is the long exact sequence of the derived functors of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$; the second is that of $R^\bullet\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$, transported along the balancing isomorphism.

Over a PID, using a free resolution $0\to F_1\to F_0\to A\to0$, the definition reduces to Quick's: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,M) = \operatorname{coker}\big(\mathrm{Hom}(F_0,M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(F_1,M)\big)$, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n = 0$ for $n\ge2$.

blocks.title: Ext over the integers
blocks.body:
For abelian groups:

1. $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}}(A,B) = 0$ for $n\ge2$.
2. $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/m,B)\cong B/mB$; in particular $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/m,\mathbb{Z}/n)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(m,n)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$.
3. $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\bigoplus_iA_i,B)\cong\prod_i\mathrm{Ext}^1(A_i,B)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\prod_jB_j)\cong\prod_j\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B_j)$ (Weibel Proposition 3.3.4).
4. If $A$ is finitely generated with torsion subgroup $T(A)$, then $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^r$ ($r$ the rank) and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong T(A)$.
5. If $A$ is a torsion group, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong A^* = \mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, the Pontryagin dual (Weibel Example 3.3.3).

1. Every abelian group has a free resolution of length one.

2. The resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/m\to0$ gives the complex $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},B)\xrightarrow{m}\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},B)$, i.e. $B\xrightarrow{m}B$ in degrees $0, 1$. Its $H^1$ is $B/mB$ (and its $H^0$ is $B[m] = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/m,B)$, as it should be). For $B = \mathbb{Z}/n$, $B/mB = \mathbb{Z}/(m,n)$.

3. A direct sum of projective resolutions is a projective resolution of the direct sum, and $\mathrm{Hom}(\bigoplus P^{(i)},B) = \prod\mathrm{Hom}(P^{(i)},B)$; cohomology commutes with products. The second statement is the same with $\mathrm{Hom}(P,\prod B_j) = \prod\mathrm{Hom}(P,B_j)$.

4. Write $A\cong\mathbb{Z}^r\oplus\bigoplus_i\mathbb{Z}/a_i$ by the structure theorem. By 3 and 2, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}/a_i\cong T(A)$, and $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^r$ since there are no non-zero maps from a finite group to $\mathbb{Z}$.

5. Use the injective resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ is the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$. A torsion group has no non-zero maps to the torsion-free group $\mathbb{Q}$, so the cokernel is all of $A^*$. For $A = \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$ this gives $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty),\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)^*\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$, the $p$-adic integers, an uncountable group: Ext of a countable group into $\mathbb{Z}$ need not be countable.

blocks.title: One Ext group, two resolutions
blocks.body: Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^i_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Z})$ by resolving the first variable, then by resolving the second, and compare the answers.
blocks.solution:
First variable: $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$; applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ gives $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $0,1$. So $\mathrm{Ext}^0 = 0$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1 = \mathbb{Z}/n$, and nothing higher.

Second variable: $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$; applying $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,-)$ gives $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ in degrees $0,1$. The first group is $0$; the second consists of homomorphisms sending $1$ to an element of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ killed by $n$, i.e. to one of $0,\frac1n,\dots,\frac{n-1}{n}$, so it is $\mathbb{Z}/n$. Again $\mathrm{Ext}^0 = 0$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$.

The two computations look nothing alike, and the fact that they agree is the balancing theorem. The Washington note on injectives and Ext treats this check as the first test of the injective-resolution definition.

blocks.title: The base ring matters
blocks.body: Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ for $R = \mathbb{Z}$, $R = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $R = \mathbb{Z}/4$.
blocks.solution:
Over $\mathbb{Z}$: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ in degrees $0$ and $1$ (by the theorem above, with $m = n = 2$), zero above.

Over $\mathbb{Z}/2$, a field: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is free, so $\mathrm{Ext}^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^n = 0$ for $n\ge1$.

Over $\mathbb{Z}/4$, use the periodic resolution $\cdots\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$. Now $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/4,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and multiplication by $2$ induces $0$ on it. So the cochain complex is $\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{0}\cdots$, and $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ for every $n\ge0$.

Same two modules, three rings, three answers. In each case $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ classifies extensions of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ by $\mathbb{Z}/2$ as modules over that ring: over $\mathbb{Z}$ and over $\mathbb{Z}/4$ the non-trivial class is $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/4\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$; over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ the group $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is not a module at all, and every extension splits.

blocks.title: Ext detects projectives and injectives
blocks.body:
1. $P$ is projective if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,M) = 0$ for all $M$.
2. $I$ is injective if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(M,I) = 0$ for all $M$, if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,I) = 0$ for every left ideal $J$.

1. If $P$ is projective, $0\to P\to P\to 0$ is a resolution, so the higher Ext vanish. Conversely, let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be exact. The long exact sequence in the second variable contains $\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(P,C)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,A) = 0$, so $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ preserves surjections.

2. The first equivalence is the same argument with the first-variable sequence: $\mathrm{Hom}(B,I)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,I)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,I) = 0$. For the second, the long exact sequence of $0\to J\to R\to R/J\to0$ gives $\mathrm{Hom}(R,I)\to\mathrm{Hom}(J,I)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,I)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(R,I) = 0$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,I) = 0$ says exactly that every map $J\to I$ extends to $R$; Baer's criterion finishes.

blocks.title: More tools for Ext
blocks.body:
1. Localisation (Weibel Proposition 3.3.10). Let $R$ be commutative Noetherian, $A$ finitely generated and $S$ multiplicative. Then $S^{-1}\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^n_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}A,S^{-1}B)$. The point is that $A$ has a resolution by finitely generated free modules, and $\mathrm{Hom}$ out of a finitely generated free (more generally finitely presented) module commutes with localisation. Consequently $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = 0$ if and only if it vanishes after localising at every maximal ideal, which is why commutative algebra papers such as Holanda-Miranda-Neto work over a Noetherian local ring from the start. Without finite generation the statement fails.
2. Module structure. For commutative $R$, $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)$ is an $R$-module, killed by $\mathrm{Ann}(A)$ and by $\mathrm{Ann}(B)$.
3. Yoneda product. Splicing exact sequences gives products $\mathrm{Ext}^m(B,C)\times\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{m+n}(A,C)$; this makes $\mathrm{Ext}^*(A,A)$ a graded ring (Wikipedia, Ext functor). For a polynomial ring over a field $k$, $\mathrm{Ext}^*(k,k)$ is an exterior algebra, the shadow of Koszul duality.
4. Dualities. Papers use several 'dual' functors built from Hom, and they should not be confused: the Pontryagin dual $A^* = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ of Weibel; the $R$-dual $M^* = \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,R)$; the Matlis dual $M^\vee = \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,E(k))$ over a local ring, with $E(k)$ the injective hull of the residue field; and the canonical dual $M^\dagger = \mathrm{Hom}_R(M,\omega_R)$ over a Cohen-Macaulay local ring with canonical module $\omega_R$. Holanda-Miranda-Neto prove dualities of the form $\mathrm{Tor}_j(M,N^\dagger)^\dagger\cong\mathrm{Ext}^j(M,N)$ under vanishing hypotheses, by playing a free resolution of $M$ against an injective resolution of $\omega_R$ in a double complex. The underlying identity is Hom-tensor adjunction, $\mathrm{Hom}(F\otimes N,E)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(F,\mathrm{Hom}(N,E))$, together with the fact that $\mathrm{Hom}(-,E)$ is exact for injective $E$, so it commutes with homology: $H_j(F_\bullet\otimes N)^\vee\cong H^j(\mathrm{Hom}(F_\bullet,N^\vee))$, i.e. $\mathrm{Tor}_j(M,N)^\vee\cong\mathrm{Ext}^j(M,N^\vee)$ for $\vee = \mathrm{Hom}(-,E)$.

blocks.title: Five readings of Ext
blocks.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B)$ is one object; the sources present it through five different doors.

items.label: Resolve the first variable
items.body: $H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet,B))$ for a projective resolution of $A$: Ext measures how far $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ is from exact. Over $\mathbb{Z}$, the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(F_0,M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(F_1,M)$ for a two-term free resolution.

items.label: Resolve the second variable
items.body: $H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet))$ for an injective resolution of $B$: Ext is the right derived functor of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$. This is the form available in any abelian category with enough injectives; Wikipedia lists sheaf cohomology as Ext in the category of sheaves.

items.label: Classes of extensions
items.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$ is the group of equivalence classes of short exact sequences $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ under Baer sum, with the split sequence as zero; $\mathrm{Ext}^n$ is classes of $n$-step exact sequences (Yoneda). This is Baer's original definition and needs no resolutions at all.

items.label: Maps to a shift
items.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = \mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathcal{A})}(A,B[n])$ in the derived category: an $n$-extension is a 'morphism of degree $n$', and the Yoneda product is composition. This is the Stacks Project definition; Tang turns to it in his Section 4.

items.label: Homotopy classes
items.body: $\mathrm{Ext}^n(X,A)$ is the set of homotopy classes of maps from $X$ into the $n$-fold delooping $B^nA$, so that higher Ext is $\pi_0$ of a mapping space.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z},\ \mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
2. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Z})\neq0$. (Use $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$ in the second variable, and show that $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is not onto.)
3. Let $R = k[x]$ and $M = k[x]/(x^2)$. Compute $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,R)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,M)$.
4. Let $R$ be commutative and $x$ a non-zero-divisor. Show $\mathrm{Ext}^1_R(R/xR,M)\cong M/xM$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(R/xR,M)\cong\{m: xm = 0\}$.
5. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}/p^2}(\mathbb{Z}/p,\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$ for all $n\ge0$.

blocks.title: Balancing: resolving either variable
blocks.body:
So far Tor and Ext were defined by resolving the first variable, and twice the page has used the balancing isomorphism that lets one resolve the second instead. This section proves it. The tool is the double complex. A (first-quadrant) double complex is a family of modules $C_{p,q}$, $p,q\ge0$, with horizontal maps $d^h\colon C_{p,q}\to C_{p-1,q}$ and vertical maps $d^v\colon C_{p,q}\to C_{p,q-1}$ such that $(d^h)^2 = 0$, $(d^v)^2 = 0$ and $d^hd^v+d^vd^h = 0$. Its total complex has $\mathrm{Tot}(C)_n = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}$ and differential $d = d^h+d^v$; the anticommutation gives $d^2 = 0$. If the squares commute instead, one inserts the sign $(-1)^p$ on the vertical maps (the sign trick of the conventions table).

The example that matters: for chain complexes $P_\bullet$ and $Q_\bullet$, the tensor double complex $C_{p,q} = P_p\otimes Q_q$ with $d^h = d\otimes1$ and $d^v = (-1)^p\,1\otimes d$. Weibel's Theorem 2.7.2 proves balance with the acyclic assembly lemma (his Lemma 2.7.3) and the mapping cone of the augmentation, and Boe's course follows the same route; that is the proof given here. The Michigan notes on Tor instead use a lemma about double complexes whose rows and columns are all exact.

blocks.title: Exact columns give an exact total complex
blocks.body: Let $C$ be a double complex with $C_{p,q} = 0$ unless $p\ge0$ and $q\ge0$, and suppose that every column $(C_{p,\bullet},d^v)$ is exact. Then $\mathrm{Tot}(C)$ is exact. (This is the first-quadrant case of Weibel's acyclic assembly Lemma 2.7.3.)

Let $x = (x_{n,0},x_{n-1,1},\dots,x_{0,n})\in\mathrm{Tot}_n$ be a cycle, with $x_{p,q}\in C_{p,q}$. Being a cycle means that for each $p+q = n-1$,
$$d^hx_{p+1,q}+d^vx_{p,q+1} = 0.$$
We remove the components one at a time, starting from the bottom row. Column $n$ is exact at $q = 0$, so $d^v\colon C_{n,1}\to C_{n,0}$ is onto, and $x_{n,0} = d^vy_{n,1}$. Replace $x$ by $x-d(y_{n,1})$; this changes $x$ only in positions $(n,0)$ and $(n-1,1)$, kills the first, and is still a cycle in the same homology class. Now $x_{n,0} = 0$, and the cycle condition at $(n-1,0)$ reads $d^vx_{n-1,1} = 0$. Column $n-1$ is exact at $q = 1$, so $x_{n-1,1} = d^vy_{n-1,2}$; subtract $d(y_{n-1,2})$, which kills the $(n-1,1)$ component and only changes $(n-2,2)$ further. Continue along the anti-diagonal. After $n+1$ steps all components are zero, so the original $x$ was $d$ of the sum of the $y$'s. The process stops because the double complex lives in the first quadrant: there are only $n+1$ components to kill.

blocks.caption: The staircase argument. A cycle in total degree n has one component on each square of the anti-diagonal. Exactness of the columns lets one kill the component on the bottom row by a vertical boundary, which only disturbs the next square up and to the left, and so on to the top.
blocks.alt: A grid of dots for a first-quadrant double complex with p horizontal and q vertical. The anti-diagonal p plus q equals 3 is highlighted, with x components at (3,0), (2,1), (1,2), (0,3). Arrows show y components one row higher being mapped down by the vertical differential and left by the horizontal one, forming a staircase from the bottom right to the top left.

blocks.title: Balancing Tor and Ext
blocks.body:
Let $P_\bullet\to A$ be a projective resolution of a right module and $Q_\bullet\to B$ one of a left module. The augmentations induce quasi-isomorphisms
$$P_\bullet\otimes B\ \xleftarrow{\ \simeq\ }\ \mathrm{Tot}(P_\bullet\otimes Q_\bullet)\ \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }\ A\otimes Q_\bullet.$$
Hence $H_n(P_\bullet\otimes B)\cong H_n(A\otimes Q_\bullet)$: Tor may be computed by resolving either variable. For $R$ commutative, $P_p\otimes Q_q\cong Q_q\otimes P_p$ gives $\mathrm{Tor}_n(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n(B,A)$. Dually, for a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ and an injective resolution $B\to I^\bullet$, the cochain complexes $\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet,B)$, $\mathrm{Tot}\,\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet,I^\bullet)$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(A,I^\bullet)$ are quasi-isomorphic, so the two definitions of Ext agree (Weibel 2.7.2 and 2.7.6).

Two facts from earlier: a chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if its mapping cone is exact (exercises of the complexes section, from the long exact sequence of $0\to D\to\operatorname{cone}\to C[-1]\to0$), and exact columns give an exact total complex.

Let $\varepsilon\colon\mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)\to P\otimes B$ be $1\otimes\eta$ on the bottom row $P_p\otimes Q_0$ and zero elsewhere, where $\eta\colon Q_0\to B$ is the augmentation. Form a new double complex $D$ by adding the row $D_{p,-1} = P_p\otimes B$ below $P\otimes Q$, with vertical maps $(-1)^p\,1\otimes\eta\colon P_p\otimes Q_0\to P_p\otimes B$. The $p$-th column of $D$ is $P_p\otimes(\cdots\to Q_1\to Q_0\to B\to0)$. This is exact: $P_p$ is projective, hence flat, and the augmented resolution is exact. After moving the row index up by one, $D$ is a first-quadrant double complex with exact columns, so $\mathrm{Tot}(D)$ is exact. But
$$\mathrm{Tot}(D)_n = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}P_p\otimes Q_q\ \oplus\ P_{n+1}\otimes B = \mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)_n\oplus(P\otimes B)_{n+1},$$
and comparing differentials shows that $\mathrm{Tot}(D)$ is the mapping cone of $\varepsilon$, shifted by one degree and with signs changed on some summands (which affects neither exactness). So the cone of $\varepsilon$ is exact and $\varepsilon$ is a quasi-isomorphism. The same argument with rows instead of columns (each row $(\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to A\to0)\otimes Q_q$ is exact because $Q_q$ is flat) gives the other quasi-isomorphism.

For commutativity, the map $P_p\otimes Q_q\to Q_q\otimes P_p$, $x\otimes y\mapsto(-1)^{pq}y\otimes x$ is an isomorphism of total complexes, and the right side computes $\mathrm{Tor}(B,A)$ by the first part. The Ext statement is proved by the same steps with $\mathrm{Hom}(P_p,I^q)$: the columns $\mathrm{Hom}(P_p,B\to I^\bullet)$ are exact because $\mathrm{Hom}(P_p,-)$ is exact, and the rows $\mathrm{Hom}(P_\bullet\to A,I^q)$ are exact because $\mathrm{Hom}(-,I^q)$ is exact.

blocks.title: The total complex in the smallest case
blocks.body: Over $\mathbb{Z}$, take $P = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{4}\mathbb{Z})\to\mathbb{Z}/4$ and $Q = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{6}\mathbb{Z})\to\mathbb{Z}/6$. Write down $\mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)$ and compute its homology.
blocks.solution:
All four terms $P_p\otimes Q_q$ are $\mathbb{Z}$. In degree $2$ there is $P_1\otimes Q_1$, in degree $1$ the sum $P_0\otimes Q_1\oplus P_1\otimes Q_0$, in degree $0$ the term $P_0\otimes Q_0$. With $d^h = 4$ and $d^v = (-1)^p\,6$:
$$\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\ e\mapsto(4,\,-6)\ }\mathbb{Z}^2\xrightarrow{\ (u,v)\mapsto 6u+4v\ }\mathbb{Z}.$$
The composite is $24-24 = 0$. $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}/(6,4) = \mathbb{Z}/2 = \mathbb{Z}/4\otimes\mathbb{Z}/6$. The kernel of $(u,v)\mapsto6u+4v$ is generated by $(2,-3)$, and the image of the first map is generated by $(4,-6) = 2(2,-3)$, so $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2 = \mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/4,\mathbb{Z}/6)$. The first map is injective, so $H_2 = 0$. Resolving only $\mathbb{Z}/4$ gives $\mathbb{Z}/6\xrightarrow{4}\mathbb{Z}/6$, and resolving only $\mathbb{Z}/6$ gives $\mathbb{Z}/4\xrightarrow{6}\mathbb{Z}/4$; both have the same homology $\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2$, as the theorem says.

blocks.title: Why the two resolutions agree
blocks.body: Balancing is the first theorem in the subject that is not a formal consequence of the definitions, and each source proves it differently.

items.label: Cone and assembly
items.body: Show that the augmentation $\mathrm{Tot}(P\otimes Q)\to P\otimes B$ has exact mapping cone, because the cone is the total complex of a double complex with exact columns (acyclic assembly). This is Weibel's proof of Theorem 2.7.2, which Boe's course follows and which is given above.

items.label: Acyclic double complex
items.body: Prove once that for a first-quadrant double complex whose rows and columns are exact except at the edge, the homology of the bottom row, of the left column and of the total complex all coincide; apply it to $P\otimes Q$. This is how the Michigan notes on Tor organise the argument.

items.label: Two spectral sequences
items.body: Filter the total complex by rows or by columns; each filtration gives a spectral sequence converging to $H(\mathrm{Tot})$, and when one family of lines is exact the spectral sequence collapses. nLab describes balanced Tor this way, and Holanda-Miranda-Neto use the same two spectral sequences on a Hom-tensor double complex to obtain Ext-Tor dualities and five-term exact sequences.

items.label: Derived category
items.body: In $D(R)$ a resolution is isomorphic to the module it resolves, so the derived tensor product $A\otimes^LB$ may be computed by replacing either or both arguments; balance becomes the statement that $P\otimes Q\to P\otimes B$ is a quasi-isomorphism when $P$ is a complex of flat modules.

blocks.body:
1. Check that $d = d^h+d^v$ squares to zero on $\mathrm{Tot}(C)$ when $d^hd^v+d^vd^h = 0$, and that the sign trick turns a commuting double complex into an anticommuting one.
2. Give an example of a double complex in the second quadrant (unbounded) with exact columns whose direct-sum total complex is not exact. Where does the staircase argument break?
3. Use balance and the resolution $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$ in the second variable to compute $\mathrm{Tor}_1(A,\mathbb{Z}/n)$ for any abelian group $A$.
4. Use the balancing theorem to derive the long exact Tor sequence in the second variable from the one in the first.

blocks.title: Extensions and Yoneda Ext
blocks.body:
An extension of $A$ by $B$ is a short exact sequence $\xi\colon 0\to B\xrightarrow{i}X\xrightarrow{\pi}A\to0$. Two extensions $\xi,\xi'$ are equivalent if there is a homomorphism $\varphi\colon X\to X'$ with $\varphi i = i'$ and $\pi'\varphi = \pi$; by the five lemma (or the snake lemma) such a $\varphi$ is automatically an isomorphism, so this is an equivalence relation. The split extension is $0\to B\to B\oplus A\to A\to0$. Write $E(A,B)$ for the set of equivalence classes. The order of the letters matters, and not every text uses this one; see the conventions table below.

The main theorem identifies $E(A,B)$ with $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$. The connecting map gives a direct description of the class: applying $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ to $\xi$ yields $\mathrm{Hom}(X,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)\xrightarrow{\delta}\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$, and the class of $\xi$ is $\delta(\mathrm{id}_B)$. The element $\mathrm{id}_B$ lies in the image of $\mathrm{Hom}(X,B)$ exactly when there is a retraction $X\to B$, i.e. when $\xi$ splits; so $\delta(\mathrm{id}_B)$ is the obstruction to splitting, and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B) = 0$ forces every extension to split (Weibel Lemma 3.4.1). The proof below uses a more hands-on description through a presentation of $A$.

blocks.title: Ext^1 classifies extensions
blocks.body:
Choose an exact sequence $0\to M\xrightarrow{j}P\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A\to0$ with $P$ projective, so that $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\cong\operatorname{coker}\big(j^*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(M,B)\big)$ by dimension shifting. There is a bijection
$$\Theta\colon E(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$$
sending the split extension to $0$. It sends $\xi$ to the class of $\beta = \tau j$, where $\tau\colon P\to X$ is any lift of $\varepsilon$ through $\pi$; its inverse sends the class of $\beta\colon M\to B$ to the pushout extension $0\to B\to X_\beta\to A\to0$, where $X_\beta = (B\oplus P)/\{(\beta(m),-j(m)) : m\in M\}$. Under $\Theta$, the group law of $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ corresponds to the Baer sum of extensions (Weibel Corollary 3.4.5).

blocks.caption: Comparing an extension with a projective presentation of A. A lift tau of epsilon restricts to beta on M; conversely the left square, for a given beta, is a pushout that builds the extension X_beta.
blocks.alt: Two short exact rows: 0 to M to P to A to 0 on top, and 0 to B to X to A to 0 below, with vertical maps beta from M to B, tau from P to X, and the identity on A.

blocks.body:
The cokernel description. The long exact sequence of $\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ for $0\to M\to P\to A\to0$ contains $\mathrm{Hom}(P,B)\xrightarrow{j^*}\mathrm{Hom}(M,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(P,B) = 0$.

$\Theta$ is well defined. A lift $\tau$ exists because $P$ is projective, and $\pi\tau j = \varepsilon j = 0$ shows that $\tau j$ lands in $i(B)$; regard it as $\beta\colon M\to B$. Two lifts differ by a map $P\to X$ with image in $\ker\pi = i(B)$, i.e. by $i\varphi$ with $\varphi\colon P\to B$, and then the two $\beta$'s differ by $\varphi j = j^*\varphi$, which is zero in the cokernel. If $\psi\colon X\to X'$ is an equivalence, $\psi\tau$ is a lift for $\xi'$ with the same restriction to $M$. So $\Theta(\xi)$ depends only on the class of $\xi$. For the split extension, take $\tau(p) = (0,\varepsilon(p))$, so $\beta = 0$.

The pushout is an extension. In $X_\beta$, put $b\mapsto[b,0]$ and $[b,p]\mapsto\varepsilon(p)$. The first is injective: $(b,0) = (\beta(m),-j(m))$ forces $j(m) = 0$, so $m = 0$ and $b = 0$. The second is well defined and onto. If $\varepsilon(p) = 0$ then $p = j(m)$ and $[b,p] = [b+\beta(m),0]$, so the kernel is the image of $B$. If $\beta' = \beta+\varphi j$ for some $\varphi\colon P\to B$, then $[b,p]\mapsto[b-\varphi(p),p]$ is an equivalence $X_\beta\to X_{\beta'}$ (it carries $(\beta(m),-j(m))$ to $(\beta(m)+\varphi j(m),-j(m)) = (\beta'(m),-j(m))$). So $\Psi[\beta] = [X_\beta]$ is a well-defined map $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)\to E(A,B)$.

They are inverse. For $X_\beta$ the map $\tau(p) = [0,p]$ lifts $\varepsilon$, and $\tau j(m) = [0,j(m)] = [\beta(m),0]$, so $\Theta\Psi[\beta] = [\beta]$. Conversely, given $\xi$ with lift $\tau$ and $\beta = \tau j$, the map $B\oplus P\to X$, $(b,p)\mapsto i(b)+\tau(p)$ vanishes on the elements $(\beta(m),-j(m))$ and so induces $X_\beta\to X$, compatible with the maps from $B$ and to $A$. It is therefore an equivalence, and $\Psi\Theta[\xi] = [\xi]$.

The statement about Baer sums is Weibel's Corollary 3.4.5 and is not proved here; Exercise 2 below asks for the key step.

blocks.title: Baer sum and Yoneda Ext
blocks.body:
Baer sum. Given extensions $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ and $0\to B\to X'\to A\to0$, form the pullback $Y = \{(x,x')\in X\oplus X' : \pi(x) = \pi'(x')\}$, which contains $B\oplus B$, and divide by the anti-diagonal $\{(i(b),-i'(b))\}$. The quotient $X''$ fits into an extension $0\to B\to X''\to A\to0$, the Baer sum. With it, $E(A,B)$ is an abelian group, the split extension is zero, and $\Theta$ is an isomorphism of groups.

Yoneda Ext. A degree $n$ Yoneda extension of $A$ by $B$ is an exact sequence $0\to B\to Z_{n-1}\to\cdots\to Z_0\to A\to0$. Two of them are called equivalent if they are related by the equivalence relation generated by maps of such sequences that are the identity on $A$ and $B$. In any abelian category, the equivalence classes form a group $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathrm{Yon}}(A,B)$, and the Stacks Project shows (its Lemma 13.27.5) that every element of $\mathrm{Ext}^n(A,B) = \mathrm{Hom}_D(A,B[n])$ comes from a Yoneda extension, with equivalent extensions giving equal elements and conversely. So Yoneda Ext agrees with derived-category Ext, and hence with derived-functor Ext when there are enough projectives or injectives. Tang's paper on profinite and solid modules starts from this comparison: it needs to know when Yoneda Ext and derived-functor Ext agree in the categories it studies, and that is where enough projectives or injectives enter.

Splicing a degree $m$ extension of $B$ by $C$ with a degree $n$ extension of $A$ by $B$ at $B$ gives a degree $m+n$ extension of $A$ by $C$; this is the Yoneda product.

blocks.title: Extensions of Z/p by Z/p
blocks.body: Let $p$ be prime. Find all extensions $0\to\mathbb{Z}/p\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/p\to0$ of abelian groups up to equivalence, and compare with the isomorphism types of $X$. (Weibel, Exercise 3.4.1.)
blocks.solution:
$\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/p,\mathbb{Z}/p)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p$, so there are exactly $p$ classes. Use the presentation $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/p\to0$: here $\mathrm{Hom}(M,B) = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/p) = \mathbb{Z}/p$, and the image of $j^*$ is $p\cdot\mathbb{Z}/p = 0$. For $\beta_k(1) = k\in\mathbb{Z}/p$ the pushout is
$$X_k = (\mathbb{Z}/p\oplus\mathbb{Z})/\langle(k,-p)\rangle.$$
For $k = 0$ this is $\mathbb{Z}/p\oplus\mathbb{Z}/p$, the split extension. For $k\ne0$ the element $[0,1]$ has $p[0,1] = [k,0]\ne0$ and $p^2[0,1] = [pk,0] = 0$, so it has order $p^2$ and $X_k\cong\mathbb{Z}/p^2$, with $B$ embedded as the subgroup of order $p$ and the quotient map $X_k\to\mathbb{Z}/p$ sending $[0,1]$ to $1$.

So there are $p$ inequivalent extensions but only two isomorphism types of middle group: $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$ once, and $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ for $p-1$ different classes. Concretely, the non-split classes are $0\to\mathbb{Z}/p\xrightarrow{1\mapsto p}\mathbb{Z}/p^2\xrightarrow{\pi_u}\mathbb{Z}/p\to0$ with $\pi_u(1) = u$ for $u\in(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$; an equivalence would be an automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ fixing $p$ (so multiplication by some $a\equiv1\bmod p$) and intertwining $\pi_u,\pi_{u'}$, forcing $u = u'$. Note also that a non-split extension cannot have middle group $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^2$: that is a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_p$, in which every subspace has a complement.

blocks.title: Who is extended by whom
blocks.body: For modules the main references agree: the sequence $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ is an extension of $A$ by $B$, quotient named first, with class in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$. The reverse phrasing also occurs, especially for groups, and at least one set of lecture notes mixes the two, so it is safest to read the variance off the exact sequence.

rows.text: An extension of $A$ by $B$ is $0\to B\to X\to A\to0$ (quotient named first), classified by $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$.
A degree $i$ Yoneda extension of $B$ by $A$ is $0\to A\to Z_{i-1}\to\cdots\to Z_0\to B\to0$, with class in $\mathrm{Ext}^i(B,A)$: again the right-hand end is named first.
An extension of $X$ by $A$ is $0\to A\to P\to X\to0$, classified by $\mathrm{Ext}^1(X,A)$; same order.

$G$ is an extension of $Q$ by $N$ when $1\to N\to G\to Q\to1$ is exact, and $H^2(G,M)$ classifies extensions of $G$ by $M$; but the group extension article notes that the reversed phrasing, 'extension of $N$ by $Q$', is also used by some authors.

Calls $0\to A\to B\to M\to0$ an extension of $M$ by $A$ (quotient first), but then writes the splitting criterion with $\mathrm{Ext}(A,M)$ for these same extensions of $M$ by $A$, and its proof (lifting $\mathrm{id}_M$ to $B\to M$) is really about sequences $0\to M\to B\to A\to0$. With the letters as in his definition, the criterion should read $\mathrm{Ext}(M,A)$; this is the kind of slip the variance check catches.

blocks.title: Homological dimension
blocks.body:
The projective dimension $\mathrm{pd}_RM$ is the smallest $n$ such that $M$ has a projective resolution of length $n$ ($\infty$ if there is none); $\mathrm{pd}\,M = 0$ means $M$ is projective. The injective dimension $\mathrm{id}_RM$ is defined dually with injective resolutions. The (left) global dimension of $R$ is $\sup_M\mathrm{pd}_RM$. Papers use these as standing hypotheses ('let $M$ have finite projective dimension'), as conclusions, and, in representation theory, as invariants of algebras: Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson need the global dimension of an exact structure to be finite for their invariants, and relate a relative global dimension of incidence algebras of grids to representation dimension.

Two consequences of the definitions are used constantly. Schanuel's lemma (Stacks Lemma 10.109.1): if $0\to K\to P\to M\to0$ and $0\to L\to P'\to M\to0$ are exact with $P,P'$ projective, then $K\oplus P'\cong L\oplus P$. So syzygies are well defined up to projective summands, and whether the $n$-th syzygy is projective does not depend on the resolution (Stacks Lemmas 10.109.3-10.109.4, Weibel Lemma 4.1.6). And dimension shifting converts a bound on $\mathrm{pd}\,M$ into the vanishing of Ext, as in the next theorem.

blocks.title: Dimension and vanishing of Ext
blocks.body:
Let $n\ge0$.

1. $\mathrm{pd}_RM\le n$ if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}_R(M,N) = 0$ for all $N$, if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(M,N) = 0$ for all $i>n$ and all $N$ (Stacks Lemma 10.109.8, Weibel Lemma 4.1.6).
2. $\mathrm{id}_RN\le n$ if and only if $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}_R(R/J,N) = 0$ for every left ideal $J$ (by Weibel's Lemma 4.1.11, the Baer form of the injectivity test, applied to a cosyzygy).
3. Consequently the global dimension of $R$ equals $\sup\{\mathrm{pd}_R(R/J)\}$ over left ideals $J$, and also equals $\sup_N\mathrm{id}_RN$ (Weibel's Global Dimension Theorem 4.1.2; Stacks Lemma 10.109.12 for the cyclic modules; Wikipedia, Global dimension).

1. If $M$ has a projective resolution of length $n$, use it to compute Ext: $\mathrm{Hom}(P_i,N) = 0$ for $i>n$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^i = 0$ for $i>n$. Conversely, suppose $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(M,-) = 0$. Take any projective resolution and let $K_{n-1} = \ker(P_{n-1}\to P_{n-2})$ (with $K_{-1} = M$, and $K_{n-1}$ the image of $P_n$). Dimension shifting along $0\to K_i\to P_i\to K_{i-1}\to0$ gives $\mathrm{Ext}^1(K_{n-1},N)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(M,N) = 0$ for all $N$ (for $n = 0$ this is the hypothesis itself). By the theorem that Ext detects projectives, $K_{n-1}$ is projective, and $0\to K_{n-1}\to P_{n-1}\to\cdots\to P_0\to M\to0$ is a projective resolution of length $n$.

2. If $\mathrm{id}\,N\le n$, compute Ext from an injective resolution of length $n$ (allowed by balancing) to get the vanishing. Conversely, take an injective resolution $0\to N\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ and let $C^{n-1}$ be the image of $I^{n-1}\to I^n$ (with $C^{-1} = N$), so that $0\to N\to I^0\to\cdots\to I^{n-1}\to C^{n-1}\to0$ is exact. Dimension shifting gives $\mathrm{Ext}^1(R/J,C^{n-1})\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(R/J,N)$, and by the Baer form of the injectivity test, $C^{n-1}$ is injective exactly when these vanish for all $J$, and then the displayed sequence is an injective resolution of length $n$.

3. If $\mathrm{pd}(R/J)\le n$ for all $J$, then $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(R/J,N) = 0$ for all $J$ and $N$, so $\mathrm{id}\,N\le n$ for every $N$ by 2. Then $\mathrm{Ext}^{n+1}(M,N) = 0$ for all $M,N$ (compute with an injective resolution of $N$ of length $n$), so $\mathrm{pd}\,M\le n$ for every $M$ by 1.

blocks.title: Dimensions of familiar rings
blocks.body: Find the global dimension of a field, of $\mathbb{Z}$, of $\mathbb{Z}/6$ and of $\mathbb{Z}/4$, and the projective dimension of $k$ over $k[x,y]$.
blocks.solution:
A field: every module is free, so the global dimension is $0$. (Global dimension $0$ means every module is projective, i.e. $R$ is semisimple; Wikipedia lists this criterion.)

$\mathbb{Z}$, or any PID that is not a field: every ideal is free, so $\mathrm{pd}(R/J)\le1$, and $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not projective, so the global dimension is $1$. Rings of global dimension at most $1$ are called hereditary.

$\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/3$ is a product of fields, hence semisimple: global dimension $0$.

$\mathbb{Z}/4$: the periodic resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ gave $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}/4}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2\neq0$ for every $n$, so $\mathrm{pd}\,\mathbb{Z}/2 = \infty$ by part 1 of the theorem, and the global dimension is infinite. This is the simplest example of a local ring that is not regular: by Serre's theorem (quoted from Wikipedia, Global dimension), a commutative Noetherian local ring has finite global dimension exactly when it is regular, and then the global dimension equals the Krull dimension.

$k$ over $k[x,y]$: the Koszul resolution has length $2$, so $\mathrm{pd}\,k\le2$; and $\mathrm{Ext}^2(k,k)$, computed from it, is $k\ne0$ (the dual complex $k\to k^2\to k$ has zero differentials). So $\mathrm{pd}\,k = 2$, consistent with Weibel's Corollary 4.4.12 for the localisation at $(x,y)$ and with Hilbert's syzygy theorem that $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has global dimension $n$.

blocks.title: Minimal resolutions over local rings
blocks.body:
Over a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak{m},k)$, finitely generated projective modules are free (Weibel Proposition 4.3.11; the Stacks Project uses this, as its Lemma 10.78.2, to prove Lemma 10.109.7 on resolutions by finite free modules), and a finitely generated module $M$ has a minimal free resolution: at each step map $R^{b}$ onto the current syzygy with $b$ the minimal number of generators. In a minimal resolution every differential has its matrix entries in $\mathfrak{m}$, so after tensoring with $k$ all differentials vanish. Therefore
$$\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(M,k)\cong k^{\beta_i},\qquad \beta_i = \operatorname{rank}F_i,$$
and the Betti numbers $\beta_i$ do not depend on the minimal resolution. In particular $\mathrm{pd}_RM = \sup\{i:\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(M,k)\neq0\}$ (Weibel Proposition 4.4.11, whose proof uses minimal generators in the same way), and $M$ is free if and only if $\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(M,k) = 0$. Freeness criteria such as those of Holanda-Miranda-Neto conclude that a finitely generated module over a local ring is free from the vanishing of suitable Ext or Tor groups; this is the simplest criterion of that kind.

Depth and maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules, which the same paper uses alongside these facts, are treated through Ext in the next section. Canonical modules and local duality are not covered on this page (see the paper's Section 1 for its conventions).

1. Prove Schanuel's lemma. (Form the pullback of $P\to M\leftarrow P'$.)
2. Show that if $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ is exact then $\mathrm{pd}\,M\le\max(\mathrm{pd}\,M',\mathrm{pd}\,M'')$.
3. Let $R = k[x]/(x^2)$. Show that every finitely generated $R$-module is free or has infinite projective dimension, and compute the Betti numbers of $k$.
4. Show that a ring of global dimension $0$ has every short exact sequence of modules split.
5. Compute the minimal free resolution and Betti numbers of $R/(x^2,xy)$ over $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $(x,y)$.

blocks.title: Depth and the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula
blocks.body:
Commutative algebra papers phrase their hypotheses through depth. Holanda and Miranda-Neto, for instance, fix the convention that the depth of a finite module over a local ring is its $\mathfrak{m}$-depth, assume in their Theorem 2.1 that $N$ is maximal Cohen-Macaulay and deduce from the vanishing of $\mathrm{Ext}^j(M,N)$ that modules built from $M$ and $N$ are again maximal Cohen-Macaulay; their freeness criteria are derived from such statements later in the paper. Depth is defined by regular sequences, but it is computed through Ext, and its main theorem, the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula, ties it to projective dimension. This section proves those homological facts. Canonical modules and local duality remain outside the page.

Throughout, $(R,\mathfrak{m},k)$ is a commutative Noetherian local ring and all modules are finitely generated. Two facts from commutative algebra are used without proof. First, Nakayama's lemma: if $M
eq0$ then $\mathfrak{m}M
eq M$, so $M/xM
eq0$ for every $x\in\mathfrak{m}$. Second, if $M
eq0$ and every element of $\mathfrak{m}$ is a zero-divisor on $M$, then some $0
eq a\in M$ satisfies $\mathfrak{m}a = 0$; in other words $\mathfrak{m}$ is an associated prime of $M$, which follows from the finiteness of the set of associated primes together with prime avoidance. Weibel records this second fact among the standard facts (4.4.7) on which his proof of Theorem 4.4.8 rests.

blocks.title: Regular sequences, depth, Cohen-Macaulay
blocks.body:
Let $M\neq0$. A sequence $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of elements of $\mathfrak{m}$ is $M$-regular if $x_1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$ and, for $i\ge2$, $x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})M$ (Weibel Definition 4.4.3). By Nakayama all the quotients $M/(x_1,\dots,x_i)M$ are non-zero. The depth of $M$, written $\operatorname{depth}M$, is the supremum of the lengths of $M$-regular sequences; the theorem below shows that it is finite and that every regular sequence which cannot be extended has exactly this length.

Weibel notes that $\operatorname{depth}R\le\dim R$ for the Krull dimension, and calls $R$ Cohen-Macaulay when equality holds. Following Wikipedia's article, a module $M$ is Cohen-Macaulay if $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim M$, and maximal Cohen-Macaulay (MCM) if moreover $\dim M = \dim R$; so an MCM module has $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim R$. For example $R = k[x]/(x^2)$ has depth $0$, since $x$ kills $x\neq0$ and so every element of $\mathfrak{m} = (x)$ is a zero-divisor; as $\dim R = 0$, it is Cohen-Macaulay. The ring $k[x,y]$ localised at $(x,y)$ has depth at least $2$, since $x,y$ is a regular sequence ($R$ is a domain and $y$ is a non-zero-divisor on $R/(x)$, a localisation of $k[y]$).

blocks.title: Depth or grade
blocks.body: The same number appears under two names, and with a choice of ideal.

rows.text: Calls the length of a maximal regular sequence on $A$ in $\mathfrak{m}$ the grade $G(A)$ (Definition 4.4.3), and states the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula as $G(R) = G(A)+\mathrm{pd}(A)$.
Writes $\operatorname{depth}(M)$ for the same number, and states the formula as $\operatorname{depth}(R) = \mathrm{pd}_R(M)+\operatorname{depth}(M)$.
Say depth, and fix in their conventions that for finite modules it always means the $\mathfrak{m}$-depth, so regular sequences are taken in the maximal ideal.

blocks.title: Depth is the first non-vanishing Ext
blocks.body:
Let $M
eq0$, and let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be an $M$-regular sequence that cannot be extended to a longer one. Then $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(k,M) = 0$ for $i<n$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(k,M)
eq0$. Consequently all non-extendable $M$-regular sequences have the same length, and
$$\operatorname{depth}M = \min\{i:\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(k,M)
eq0\}.$$
(Weibel Theorem 4.4.8; the Stacks Project uses the same description as its Lemma 10.72.5.)

Two observations first. (a) If some $x\in\mathfrak{m}$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$, then $\mathrm{Hom}(k,M) = 0$: a homomorphism $k\to M$ sends $1$ to an element $a$ with $\mathfrak{m}a = 0$, so $xa = 0$ and hence $a = 0$. (b) For $x\in\mathfrak{m}$, the map $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)$ induced by multiplication by $x$ on $M$ is multiplication by $x$ in the $R$-module $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)$, and that module is killed by $\mathrm{Ann}(k) = \mathfrak{m}$ (the module-structure remark in the section on more tools for Ext). So the induced map is zero.

Induct on $n$. If $n = 0$, no element of $\mathfrak{m}$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$, so by the second quoted fact some $a\neq0$ has $\mathfrak{m}a = 0$, and $1\mapsto a$ is a non-zero homomorphism $k\to M$. Thus $\mathrm{Ext}^0(k,M)\neq0$.

Let $n\ge1$, put $x = x_1$ and $\bar M = M/xM$, which is non-zero. The sequence $x_2,\dots,x_n$ is $\bar M$-regular and cannot be extended, since an extension would extend $x_1,\dots,x_n$. By induction $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,\bar M) = 0$ for $i<n-1$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{n-1}(k,\bar M)\neq0$. Apply $\mathrm{Hom}(k,-)$ to $0\to M\xrightarrow{x}M\to\bar M\to0$. In the long exact sequence every map induced by $x$ is zero by (b), so the sequence breaks into short exact sequences
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,\bar M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,M)\to0\qquad(i\ge0).$$
For $i<n-1$ the middle term is zero, hence so are $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,M)$; together with $\mathrm{Hom}(k,M) = 0$ from (a), this gives $\mathrm{Ext}^j(k,M) = 0$ for all $j\le n-1$. For $i = n-1$ the left term is therefore zero, so $\mathrm{Ext}^n(k,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{n-1}(k,\bar M)\neq0$.

So the length $n$ of any non-extendable regular sequence equals $\min\{i:\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\neq0\}$, a number that does not refer to the sequence. Finally, every $M$-regular sequence can be extended until it cannot be extended further: if $x_{i+1}$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/(x_1,\dots,x_i)M\neq0$, then $x_{i+1}\notin(x_1,\dots,x_i)$, because elements of that ideal kill the quotient; so the ideals $(x_1,\dots,x_i)$ increase strictly, and since $R$ is Noetherian the process stops. Hence no regular sequence is longer than $n$, and the depth, defined as a supremum, equals this minimum.

blocks.title: Depth lemma

blocks.body:
As in the Stacks Project, apply $\mathrm{Hom}(k,-)$ and use the Ext description of depth. The long exact sequence contains the segments
$$\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N')\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N''),\qquad \mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N'')\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,N'),$$
$$\mathrm{Ext}^{i-1}(k,N'')\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N')\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N),$$
with $\mathrm{Ext}^{-1} = 0$. In each, if both outer terms vanish so does the middle one. For 1, take $i<\min\{\operatorname{depth}N',\operatorname{depth}N''\}$ in the first segment. For 2, take $i<\min\{\operatorname{depth}N,\operatorname{depth}N'-1\}$ in the second: then $i<\operatorname{depth}N$ and $i+1<\operatorname{depth}N'$. For 3, take $i<\min\{\operatorname{depth}N,\operatorname{depth}N''+1\}$ in the third: then $i-1<\operatorname{depth}N''$ and $i<\operatorname{depth}N$. In each case all $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$ of the module in question vanish below the stated bound, which is the claim.

blocks.title: Auslander-Buchsbaum formula
blocks.body:
Let $M\neq0$ be a finitely generated $R$-module of finite projective dimension. Then
$$\mathrm{pd}_RM+\operatorname{depth}M = \operatorname{depth}R.$$
(Stacks Proposition 10.111.1; Weibel Theorem 4.4.15.) In particular $\mathrm{pd}_RM\le\operatorname{depth}R$. If $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay and $\mathrm{pd}_RM<\infty$, then $M$ is maximal Cohen-Macaulay if and only if $M$ is free.

Both sources argue by induction. The Stacks Project inducts on $\operatorname{depth}M$: when it is positive it divides out an element regular on both $R$ and $M$, and in the base case $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$ it splits a minimal free resolution into short exact sequences and applies the depth lemma to them. Weibel uses a double induction on $G(R)$ and $G(A)$, with his change-of-rings theorems. The argument given here is a different arrangement: it inducts on $\mathrm{pd}M$, and uses only the Ext description of depth together with the fact that the differentials of a minimal resolution have entries in $\mathfrak{m}$.

Write $d = \operatorname{depth}R$ and $n = \mathrm{pd}M$. Take a minimal free resolution $0\to F_n\to\cdots\to F_0\to M\to0$ as in the section on minimal resolutions: $F_i\cong R^{\beta_i}$ with $\beta_i = \dim_k\mathrm{Tor}_i(M,k)$, so it has length $n$ and $F_n\neq0$, and every differential has matrix entries in $\mathfrak{m}$. Two remarks. Since $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$ is additive, $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,R^b)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,R)^b$, which for $b\ge1$ vanishes for $i<d$ and not for $i = d$. And a homomorphism $\varphi\colon R^b\to R^c$ whose matrix has entries in $\mathfrak{m}$ induces the zero map on each $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$: the induced map is the matrix of the maps induced by multiplication by the entries, which vanish by observation (b) of the previous proof.

Case $n = 0$. Then $M\cong R^{\beta_0}$ with $\beta_0\ge1$, and $\operatorname{depth}M = d$.

Case $n = 1$. The resolution is $0\to F_1\xrightarrow{\varphi}F_0\to M\to0$ with $F_1\neq0$ and $\varphi$ having entries in $\mathfrak{m}$. All maps induced by $\varphi$ in the long exact Ext sequence vanish, so it breaks into short exact sequences
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,F_0)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,F_1)\to0\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and moreover $\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_1) = 0$, because $\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_1)\to\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_0)$ is injective (left exactness) and zero. Since $F_1\neq0$, this forces $d\ge1$. Now $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M) = 0$ exactly when $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,R)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,R)$ both vanish, that is, when $i+1<d$. Hence $\operatorname{depth}M = d-1$.

Case $n\ge2$. Let $K = \operatorname{im}(F_1\to F_0)$. Then $K\neq0$ (otherwise $M\cong F_0$ would be free), $0\to K\to F_0\to M\to0$ is exact, and $0\to F_n\to\cdots\to F_1\to K\to0$ is a minimal free resolution of $K$ with $F_n\neq0$, so $\mathrm{pd}K = n-1$ by the Tor criterion for projective dimension. By induction $\operatorname{depth}K = d-n+1$, so in particular $d\ge n-1\ge1$. In the exact segment
$$\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,F_0)\to\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,K)\to\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,F_0)$$
the outer terms vanish when $i+1<d$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M)\cong\mathrm{Ext}^{i+1}(k,K)$ for $0\le i\le d-2$. The case $d = n-1$ is impossible: it would give $\operatorname{depth}K = 0$, so $\mathrm{Hom}(k,K)\neq0$, whereas $\mathrm{Hom}(k,K)$ embeds in $\mathrm{Hom}(k,F_0)$, which is $0$ because $d\ge1$. So $d\ge n$, hence $d-n\le d-2$, and for $0\le i\le d-n$ the isomorphism gives $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,M) = 0$ for $i<d-n$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^{d-n}(k,M)\neq0$. So $\operatorname{depth}M = d-n$.

Consequences. As $\operatorname{depth}M\ge0$, $\mathrm{pd}M\le d$. If $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay and $M$ is MCM of finite projective dimension, then $\operatorname{depth}M = \dim R = \operatorname{depth}R$, so $\mathrm{pd}M = 0$ and $M$ is projective, hence free over the local ring $R$. Conversely $R^b$ with $b\ge1$ has depth $\operatorname{depth}R = \dim R$ and dimension $\dim R$, so it is MCM.

blocks.title: Three ways to compute depth
blocks.body: The sources give three descriptions of the same number for a finitely generated $M\neq0$ over a Noetherian local ring.

items.label: Regular sequences
items.body: The length of a longest $M$-regular sequence in $\mathfrak{m}$: how many successive non-zero-divisors one can divide out before every element of $\mathfrak{m}$ becomes a zero-divisor. This is the definition, and it is the description in which the comparison $\operatorname{depth}\le\dim$ and the notion of a Cohen-Macaulay ring are stated.

items.label: First non-zero Ext
items.body: The smallest $i$ with $\mathrm{Ext}^i_R(k,M)\neq0$. This is the form used in proofs, because Ext has long exact sequences: the depth lemma and the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula above are both read off from it.

items.label: Local cohomology
items.body: Weibel's Theorem 4.6.3: the depth is the smallest $n$ with $H^n_{\mathfrak{m}}(M)\neq0$, where $H^n_{\mathfrak{m}}$ are the right derived functors of the $\mathfrak{m}$-torsion functor $M\mapsto\{a: \mathfrak{m}^ja = 0\text{ for some }j\}$. Weibel deduces it from the Ext description by comparing $\mathrm{Ext}(R/\mathfrak{m}^j,M)$ for growing $j$ and passing to the limit.

blocks.title: Checking Auslander-Buchsbaum over k[x,y]
blocks.body: Let $R = k[x,y]$ localised at $\mathfrak{m} = (x,y)$. Compute depth and projective dimension of $R$, $R/(x)$, $k$ and $M = R/(x^2,xy)$, and check the formula.
blocks.solution:
Depth via Ext: the Koszul complex $0\to R\to R^2\to R\to k\to0$ of the Tor section is a free resolution of $k$, so $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,N)$ is the cohomology of $N\to N^2\to N$, $n\mapsto(xn,yn)$, $(a,b)\mapsto -ya+xb$. Its $H^0$ is the socle $\{n:\mathfrak{m}n = 0\}$ and its $H^2$ is $N/\mathfrak{m}N$.

1. $R$: free, so $\mathrm{pd} = 0$; $x,y$ is regular and $R/(x,y) = k$ has depth $0$, so $\operatorname{depth}R = 2$. Formula: $0+2 = 2$.
2. $R/(x)$: resolution $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to R/(x)\to0$, so $\mathrm{pd} = 1$ (it is not free, being killed by $x$). In the Koszul cochain complex for $N = R/(x)$, a localisation of $k[y]$, the socle is $0$ and $H^1 = \{(0,b)\}/\{(0,yn)\}\cong k\neq0$, so the depth is $1$ ($y$ is regular, and nothing more). Formula: $1+1 = 2$.
3. $k$: the Koszul resolution has length $2$, and $\mathrm{pd}k = 2$ as computed in the dimension examples; the socle of $k$ is $k$, so the depth is $0$. Formula: $2+0 = 2$.
4. $M = R/(x^2,xy)$. The map $(a,b)\mapsto x^2a+xyb = x(xa+yb)$ has kernel $\{(a,b): xa+yb = 0\} = R\cdot(y,-x)$, since $R$ is a factorial domain and $x$, $y$ are coprime. So
$$0\to R\xrightarrow{\binom{y}{-x}}R^2\xrightarrow{(x^2\ \ xy)}R\to M\to0$$
is a minimal free resolution, and $\mathrm{pd}M = 2$. The class of $x$ is non-zero in $M$ but $x\cdot x$ and $y\cdot x$ lie in $(x^2,xy)$, so $x$ spans a non-zero socle element and $\operatorname{depth}M = 0$. Formula: $2+0 = 2$. Note that $M$ is not killed by any power of $\mathfrak{m}$ (the powers of $y$ survive), so depth $0$ does not require finite length.

blocks.body:
1. Let $x\in\mathfrak{m}$ be a non-zero-divisor on $M\neq0$. Show $\operatorname{depth}M/xM = \operatorname{depth}M-1$.
2. Let $R = k[x,y,z]$ localised at $(x,y,z)$ and $M = R/(x,y)$. Compute $\mathrm{pd}M$ and $\operatorname{depth}M$ and check the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula.
3. Let $0\to K\to F\to M\to0$ be exact with $F$ free and $\operatorname{depth}M<\operatorname{depth}R$. Use the depth lemma to show $\operatorname{depth}K = \operatorname{depth}M+1$.
4. Suppose $\operatorname{depth}R = 0$. Show, both from the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula and directly from a minimal free resolution and a non-zero socle element of $R$, that every finitely generated module of finite projective dimension is free.
5. Let $R$ be Cohen-Macaulay and $M\neq0$ of finite projective dimension. Show that for $0\le j\le\mathrm{pd}M$ the $j$-th syzygy of $M$ in a minimal free resolution has depth $\operatorname{depth}M+j$, and that it is maximal Cohen-Macaulay only for $j = \mathrm{pd}M$.

blocks.title: Universal coefficient theorems and extension problems
blocks.body: For a space $X$, singular homology with coefficients is the homology of $C_\bullet(X)\otimes M$, and cohomology is that of $\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet(X),M)$. The chain groups are free abelian, so the question 'how does $H_n(C\otimes M)$ depend on $H_\bullet(C)$?' is purely algebraic, and Tor and Ext answer it. These were the first applications of the two functors, and they are what the [[cohomology]] page will need.

blocks.title: Universal coefficient theorems
blocks.body:
Let $C_\bullet$ be a chain complex of free abelian groups and $M$ an abelian group. There are natural short exact sequences
$$0\to H_n(C)\otimes M\to H_n(C\otimes M)\to\mathrm{Tor}(H_{n-1}(C),M)\to0,$$
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(C),M)\to H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(C,M))\to\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(C),M)\to0.$$
Both split, but the splittings are not natural. (Weibel Theorems 3.6.2 and 3.6.5; more generally the first holds over any ring for a complex of flat modules with flat boundaries, as a Künneth theorem, Weibel 3.6.1.)

Write $Z_n = \ker d_n$ and $B_{n-1} = \operatorname{im}d_n\subseteq C_{n-1}$. Both are subgroups of free abelian groups, hence free. The sequence $0\to Z_n\to C_n\xrightarrow{d}B_{n-1}\to0$ is a short exact sequence of complexes if $Z$ and $B$ are given zero differential, and it splits in each degree since $B_{n-1}$ is free. Tensoring with $M$ therefore keeps it exact, and the long exact homology sequence reads
$$\cdots\to B_n\otimes M\xrightarrow{\ \iota_n\otimes1\ }Z_n\otimes M\to H_n(C\otimes M)\to B_{n-1}\otimes M\xrightarrow{\ \iota_{n-1}\otimes1\ }Z_{n-1}\otimes M\to\cdots,$$
where one checks that the connecting map is $\iota\otimes1$ for the inclusion $\iota\colon B\to Z$. This gives
$$0\to\operatorname{coker}(\iota_n\otimes1)\to H_n(C\otimes M)\to\ker(\iota_{n-1}\otimes1)\to0.$$
Now $0\to B_n\xrightarrow{\iota_n}Z_n\to H_n(C)\to0$ is a free resolution of $H_n(C)$. By right exactness the cokernel of $\iota_n\otimes1$ is $H_n(C)\otimes M$, and by definition of Tor the kernel of $\iota_{n-1}\otimes1$ is $\mathrm{Tor}(H_{n-1}(C),M)$.

Splitting: since $B_{n-1}$ is free, $C_n\cong Z_n\oplus B_{n-1}$; a retraction $C_n\to Z_n$ composed with $Z_n\to H_n(C)$ gives a map from $C\otimes M$ that splits the first sequence. The retraction is a choice, which is why the splitting is not natural.

The cohomology version is the same argument with $\mathrm{Hom}(-,M)$, which also preserves the degreewise split sequences; the cokernel of $\iota^*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(Z_{n-1},M)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B_{n-1},M)$ is $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(C),M)$ by definition, and the kernel of $\iota_n^*$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(C),M)$ by left exactness.

blocks.title: Cohomology of the Klein bottle from its homology
blocks.body: The [[homology]] page computed $H_0(K) = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1(K) = \mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2(K) = 0$ for the Klein bottle. Find $H^n(K;\mathbb{Z})$, $H_n(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and $H^n(K;\mathbb{Z}/2)$.
blocks.solution:
Integral cohomology, by the second sequence: $H^0 = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$. $H^1 = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$. $H^2 = \mathrm{Hom}(0,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. This is Quick's rule $H^n\cong H_n/T_n\oplus T_{n-1}$: torsion moves up one degree.

Mod $2$ homology, by the first: $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}/2$; $H_1 = (\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathrm{Tor}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$; $H_2 = 0\oplus\mathrm{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. Mod $2$ cohomology: $H^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H^1 = \mathrm{Hom}(H_1,\mathbb{Z}/2)\oplus\mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, $H^2 = \mathrm{Ext}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$.

So with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients the Klein bottle has a top class, $H_2(K;\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, as every closed surface does mod $2$, and its Betti numbers mod $2$ are $1,2,1$, those of the torus. The direct check: the chain complex from the homology page has $\partial_1 = 0$ and $\partial_2(U) = a+b-c$, $\partial_2(L) = -a+b+c$; mod $2$ both images equal $a+b+c$, so $\partial_2$ has rank $1$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and the dimensions are $1$, $3-1 = 2$, $2-1 = 1$.

blocks.title: Künneth formula for a tensor product of complexes
blocks.body:
Let $P$ be a chain complex of free abelian groups and $Q$ any chain complex of abelian groups. The tensor product complex has $(P\otimes Q)_n = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}P_p\otimes Q_q$ and $d(a\otimes b) = da\otimes b+(-1)^pa\otimes db$ for $a\in P_p$. For every $n$ there is a short exact sequence
$$0\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)\to H_n(P\otimes Q)\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\mathrm{Tor}(H_p(P),H_q(Q))\to0,$$
and it splits, though not naturally. (Weibel Theorem 3.6.3, stated there over any ring for $P$ with $P_n$ and $d(P_n)$ flat; the splitting is asserted for free complexes over $\mathbb{Z}$.) Taking $Q = M$ in degree $0$ recovers the first universal coefficient sequence.

Weibel's proof is that of the universal coefficient theorem with $Q$ in place of $M$. Put $Z_p = \ker d_p$ and $B_p = \operatorname{im}d_{p+1}\subseteq Z_p$, both free as subgroups of free groups. Give $Z$ and $B$ the zero differential, and let $B^-$ denote $B$ moved up one degree, $B^-_p = B_{p-1}$. Then $d$ defines a chain map $P\to B^-$, and $0\to Z\to P\to B^-\to0$ is a short exact sequence of complexes, split in each degree because $B_{p-1}$ is free. Tensoring with $Q$ therefore keeps it exact:
$$0\to Z\otimes Q\to P\otimes Q\to B^-\otimes Q\to0.$$
As $Z$ has zero differential, $Z\otimes Q$ is the direct sum over $p$ of the complexes $Z_p\otimes Q$ (shifted by $p$, with differential $\pm1\otimes d$), and $Z_p\otimes-$ is exact because $Z_p$ is free, so it commutes with homology: $H_n(Z\otimes Q) = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}Z_p\otimes H_q(Q)$. In the same way $H_{n+1}(B^-\otimes Q) = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}B_p\otimes H_q(Q)$.

The connecting map $H_{n+1}(B^-\otimes Q)\to H_n(Z\otimes Q)$ is $\iota\otimes1$ on each summand, for the inclusion $\iota\colon B_p\to Z_p$: given $b\otimes z$ with $b\in B_p$ and $z$ a cycle of $Q_q$, lift it to $c\otimes z$ with $dc = b$, and apply $d$ to get $b\otimes z\pm c\otimes dz = b\otimes z$. By the long exact sequence, $H_n(P\otimes Q)$ sits in a short exact sequence between the cokernel of $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\iota\otimes1$ and the kernel of $\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\iota\otimes1$ (the splicing statement proved in the section on Ext into the integers). Since $0\to B_p\to Z_p\to H_p(P)\to0$ is a free resolution, the cokernel of $\iota\otimes1\colon B_p\otimes H_q(Q)\to Z_p\otimes H_q(Q)$ is $H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)$ by right exactness, and its kernel is $\mathrm{Tor}(H_p(P),H_q(Q))$ by definition. For the splitting (exercise), first suppose $Q$ is free too. Retractions $P_p\to Z_p$ and $Q_q\to Z_q(Q)$ exist because the boundaries are free, and composing them with the projections to homology gives chain maps $P\to H(P)$ and $Q\to H(Q)$ into complexes with zero differential; their tensor product induces $H_n(P\otimes Q)\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)$, which is a left inverse of the first map. For general $Q$, choose for each $q$ a free resolution $0\to R_q\to E_q\to H_q(Q)\to0$, lift $E_q\to H_q(Q)$ to $E_q\to Z_q(Q)$ and then $R_q\to Q_{q+1}$; this gives a complex of free groups $Q'$ with a quasi-isomorphism $Q'\to Q$, and by naturality of the sequence and the five lemma $H_n(P\otimes Q')\cong H_n(P\otimes Q)$ compatibly with both outer terms. A retraction of $P_p\to Z_p$ alone does not suffice when $Q$ is not free, because $H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)\to H_q(H_p(P)\otimes Q)$ need not be injective.

blocks.title: A tensor square with a Tor class
blocks.body: Let $C$ be the complex $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $2,1,0$, the cellular chain complex of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ used in the exercises below, with $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2 = 0$. Compute $H_n(C\otimes C)$.
blocks.solution:
By the Künneth formula, the tensor part in degree $n$ is $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p\otimes H_q$ and the Tor part is $\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\mathrm{Tor}(H_p,H_q)$; only $\mathrm{Tor}(H_1,H_1) = \mathrm{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ is non-zero among the Tor groups, since $H_0$ is free and $H_2 = 0$.

$H_0 = \mathbb{Z}\otimes\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$. $H_1 = H_0\otimes H_1\oplus H_1\otimes H_0 = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$. $H_2 = H_1\otimes H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, with no Tor contribution. $H_3$: the tensor part $H_1\otimes H_2\oplus H_2\otimes H_1$ is $0$, and the Tor part is $\mathrm{Tor}(H_1,H_1) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. $H_4 = 0$.

So $H_\bullet(C\otimes C) = \mathbb{Z},(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2,\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2,0$. The class in degree $3$ is invisible to $H_\bullet(C)\otimes H_\bullet(C)$: with $e_i$ the generator of $C_i$, the element $e_2\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_2$ has boundary $2e_1\otimes e_1-2e_1\otimes e_1 = 0$ by the sign rule, while $d(e_2\otimes e_2) = 2(e_1\otimes e_2+e_2\otimes e_1)$, so it is a cycle of order $2$. The checks confirm the whole computation with a Smith normal form. The topological Künneth theorem for a product of spaces needs, in addition, that the chains on $X\times Y$ are chain equivalent to the tensor product of the chains; that belongs to the [[cohomology]] page.

blocks.body:
1. Using the homology of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ ($\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}/2$, $0$), compute $H^n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})$, $H_n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and $H^n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Q})$.
2. Show that if $H_\bullet(C)$ is finitely generated in each degree then $H^n(C;\mathbb{Z})\cong F_n\oplus T_{n-1}$, with $F_n$ the free part of $H_n$ and $T_{n-1}$ the torsion of $H_{n-1}$.
3. Show that a chain map of free complexes inducing isomorphisms on homology induces isomorphisms on cohomology with any coefficients (use naturality and the five lemma).
4. Find a space or a chain complex of free abelian groups for which no splitting of the universal coefficient sequence is natural with respect to all chain maps. (Hint: consider maps between $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}$ and its shifts.)
5. Use the Künneth formula to compute $H_\bullet(C\otimes D)$ for $C = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{4}\mathbb{Z})$ and $D = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{6}\mathbb{Z})$, both in degrees $1,0$, and compare with the total-complex example in the balancing section.
6. Prove that the Künneth sequence splits when $P$ is a complex of free abelian groups.

blocks.title: Extension problems
blocks.body:
Long exact sequences determine groups only up to extension. If a computation produces $0\to A\to X\to C\to0$ with $A$ and $C$ known, then $X$ is determined by a class in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,A)$, and further information is needed to say which. The Smith fiber sequence paper is a good example of how this appears in research: it computes bordism groups from a long exact sequence, and in its Appendix A and in examples such as Example 6.14 it has to decide whether the resulting extensions split, and meets non-split ones.

The smallest instance: from $0\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ alone one cannot tell $X = \mathbb{Z}/4$ from $X = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, because $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ has two elements. By contrast, if the outer terms have coprime orders, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,A) = 0$ and the extension splits: for example $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/3) = \mathbb{Z}/\gcd(2,3) = 0$, so any $X$ in $0\to\mathbb{Z}/3\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ is $\mathbb{Z}/6$. The same paper also uses Anderson duality of spectra; the part of it that is homological algebra, a short exact sequence with an Ext term, is the subject of the next section.

1. Find all abelian groups $X$ that fit into an exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}/4\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$, and say which of them arise from more than one class in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/4)$.
2. Suppose a long exact sequence yields $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to X\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$. Which groups $X$ are possible?
3. Show that if $\gcd(|A|,|C|) = 1$ for finite abelian $A$, $C$, then every extension of $C$ by $A$ splits.

blocks.title: Ext into the integers and Anderson duality
blocks.body:
The Smith fiber sequence paper classifies invertible field theories by the Anderson dual of bordism, $I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^\ast_\xi$, and obtains its long exact sequence of invertible field theories by Anderson-dualising the Smith fibre sequence of spectra (its Section 1, Equation (1.6); its footnote 2 refers to its Section 8.2.2 and to Freed-Hopkins for Anderson duality). The spectra are outside this page, but the homological algebra in Anderson duality is one short exact sequence whose outer terms are $\mathrm{Ext}^1(-,\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$. This section derives it, following Stojanoska's account of Anderson duality (Section 2 of her paper on duality for topological modular forms), and then compares it with the form in which Krulewski's thesis states it (Section 2.4.2, which its author says is modified from Section 8.2.2 of the Smith paper).

The input from topology is as follows. Because $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is an injective abelian group, $X\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-\ast}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is a cohomology theory on spectra, represented by the Brown-Comenetz spectrum $I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}$; likewise $\mathbb{Q}$ gives $I_{\mathbb{Q}}$. The quotient $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ induces a map $I_{\mathbb{Q}}\to I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}$, and the Anderson dual $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ is its fibre (Stojanoska, following Anderson and Hopkins-Singer). Writing $I_{\mathbb{Z}}X$ for maps from $X$ into $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$, and similarly for the others, one has $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}}X = \mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q})$ and $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X = \mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, and the fibre sequence $I_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to I_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X$ has a long exact sequence of homotopy groups in which $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X$ is composition with $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$. Everything else is algebra.

blocks.title: Hom and Ext into Z, and Anderson's sequence
blocks.body:
1. For every abelian group $A$ the sequence
$$0\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\ \varphi_A\ }\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})\to0$$
is exact, where $\varphi_A$ is composition with $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$.
2. (Splicing.) If $A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\xrightarrow{h}D\xrightarrow{k}E$ is exact, then $g$ and $h$ induce a short exact sequence $0\to\operatorname{coker}f\to C\to\ker k\to0$.
3. (Stojanoska, Section 2.) For every spectrum $X$ and every integer $t$ there is a short exact sequence
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Z})\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Z})\to0.$$
In terms of $[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}] = \pi_{-m}I_{\mathbb{Z}}X$, the group of degree $m$ classes in the cohomology theory $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$, it reads
$$0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{Z})\to[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}]\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_mX,\mathbb{Z})\to0,$$
which with $m = n+2$ is the sequence in Krulewski's Equation (2.4.19), except that Krulewski writes the first term as the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{n+1}X,\mathbb{C}^\times)$; the two agree when $\pi_{n+1}X$ is finite (see the pitfall below). If $\pi_mX$ is finitely generated, the sequence splits, non-canonically.

1. $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ are divisible, hence injective by Baer's criterion, so $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is an injective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}$. Applying $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ to it gives the two-term complex $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\varphi_A}\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, whose cohomology is $\mathrm{Ext}^0(A,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{Z})$ in degree $0$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ in degree $1$ (Ext may be computed by resolving either variable, by balancing). That is the claim; this is the computation made for $A = \mathbb{Z}/n$ in the example with two resolutions.

2. Since $gf = 0$, $g$ induces $\bar g\colon\operatorname{coker}f\to C$, injective because $\ker g = \operatorname{im}f$. Its image is $\operatorname{im}g = \ker h$. Finally $h$ maps $C$ onto $\operatorname{im}h = \ker k$.

3. The long exact sequence of the fibre sequence contains
$$\pi_{t+1}I_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to\pi_{t+1}I_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}}X\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}X,$$
that is,
$$\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\to\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}).$$
By 2, $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X$ is an extension of the kernel of the second $\varphi$ by the cokernel of the first, and by 1 these are $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t}X,\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Z})$. Put $t = -m$ for the second form. If $\pi_mX\cong\mathbb{Z}^r\oplus T$ with $T$ finite, then $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_mX,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}^r$ is free; choosing preimages of a basis gives a section, and the choice is what makes the splitting non-canonical.

blocks.title: Spin invertible field theories, algebraically
blocks.body: Krulewski's Theorem 2.4.21 (after Freed-Hopkins and Grady) identifies deformation classes of reflection-positive invertible field theories of dimension $n$ on spin manifolds with $[MTSpin,\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$, and the Pontryagin-Thom theorem (Theorem 2.18 of the Smith paper) identifies $\pi_mMTSpin$ with the spin bordism group $\Omega^{Spin}_m$. Taking as given the groups listed in Krulewski's Example 2.2.45, $\Omega^{Spin}_m = \mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z},0,0,0,\mathbb{Z}^2$ for $m = 0,\dots,8$, compute these groups for $n = 0,\dots,7$.
blocks.solution:
With $m = n+1$ the sequence reads $0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\Omega^{Spin}_n,\mathbb{Z})\to[MTSpin,\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]\to\mathrm{Hom}(\Omega^{Spin}_{n+1},\mathbb{Z})\to0$, and it splits because the right-hand group is free. Use $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^r,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}^r$.

- $n = 0$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = 0$.
- $n = 1$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$.
- $n = 2$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(0,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$.
- $n = 3$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(0,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}$.
- $n = 4,5,6$: $0$.
- $n = 7$: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(0,\mathbb{Z})\oplus\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}^2$.

The pattern is the one of the universal coefficient theorem for cohomology: the torsion of $\Omega_n$ appears in degree $n$, while the free part of $\Omega_{n+1}$ appears one degree lower; so in the group that Krulewski abbreviates as $\mho^n_\xi$ (Notation 2.4.22), indexed by the dimension $n$ of the field theories, the torsion comes from $\Omega_n$ and the free part from $\Omega_{n+1}$. In his Section 2.5.1, where the sequence is used for anomaly theories, he interprets the free quotient through anomaly polynomials (the local anomaly, visible perturbatively) and the torsion subgroup as the topological theories (the global anomaly). The group-theoretic step is only the short exact sequence and its splitting.

blocks.body:
- Krulewski states the first term of the sequence as the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{C}^\times)$, characters with values in $\mathbb{C}^\times$, where Stojanoska has $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{Z})$. They agree when $A = \pi_{m-1}X$ is finite: the exponential sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}^\times\to0$, $z\mapsto e^{2\pi iz}$, is an injective resolution of $\mathbb{Z}$ (both $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{C}^\times$ are divisible), so $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$ is the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C}^\times)$, and for finite $A$ the group $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C})$ is $0$ while $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C}^\times)$ is finite. In general they differ, already for finitely generated groups with a free part: $\mathrm{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}) = 0$, but the torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{C}^\times) = \mathbb{C}^\times$ is the infinite group of all roots of unity. So Krulewski's form is correct when $\pi_{m-1}X$ is finite, as for the bordism groups in his applications that feed this term; to compute in general, use the Ext form.
- $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ is not exact, so a long exact sequence of bordism groups does not dualise term by term: applied to $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ it gives $0\to0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}$, which is not onto at the end. The Smith paper instead obtains its long exact sequence (1.6) by taking Anderson duals of a fibre sequence of spectra, where the Ext terms are built in. By contrast $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ is exact, so Pontryagin duality does turn exact sequences of groups into exact sequences.

1. Let $A = \mathbb{Z}^r\oplus T$ with $T$ finite. Show that the cokernel of $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C})\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb{C}^\times)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Hom}(T,\mathbb{C}^\times)$, and hence to $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,\mathbb{Z})$.
2. Suppose $\pi_{m-1}X\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\pi_mX\cong\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}^2$. Compute $[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}]$.
3. Show that if every homotopy group of $X$ is finite, then $\pi_tI_{\mathbb{Z}}X\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-t-1}X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$: for such $X$ Anderson duality is Brown-Comenetz duality shifted by one.
4. Prove that $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$ takes exact sequences of abelian groups to exact sequences, and use the long exact Ext sequence to describe exactly how far $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ is from doing so on $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$.
5.
