blocks.title: Group cohomology as Ext
blocks.body:
A $G$-module is an abelian group with a $G$-action, i.e. a module over the group ring $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ (see [[group-representations]] for the same idea over a field). The trivial module $\mathbb{Z}$ has every $g$ acting as the identity. For any $G$-module $M$,
$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M) = M^G,\qquad \mathbb{Z}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}M = M_G = M/\langle gm-m\rangle,$$
the invariants and the coinvariants (the second is Arapura's Lemma 5.29). Invariants are left exact and coinvariants right exact, and their derived functors are group cohomology and homology:
$$H^n(G,M) = \mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M),\qquad H_n(G,M) = \mathrm{Tor}_n^{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M).$$
The low degrees have classical meanings (Wikipedia, Group cohomology; Arapura Theorem 5.31): $H^0 = M^G$; $H^1(G,M)$ is crossed homomorphisms $f(gh) = f(g)+gf(h)$ modulo the principal ones $f(g) = gm-m$, so $H^1(G,M) = \mathrm{Hom}(G,M)$ for trivial action; $H^2(G,M)$ classifies extensions $1\to M\to E\to G\to1$ inducing the given action; and $H_1(G,\mathbb{Z})\cong G/[G,G]$. The same formula with a commutative ring $R$ in place of $\mathbb{Z}$, $H^n(G,A) = \mathrm{Ext}^n_{R[G]}(R,A)$, is the starting point of Tang's comparison of continuous cohomology of profinite groups with its solid analogue, and the Washington note derives it exactly as here, from $M^G = \mathrm{Hom}_{KG}(K,M)$.

blocks.title: Cohomology of a cyclic group
blocks.body: Let $G = C_n = \langle t\rangle$. Using the periodic resolution from the resolutions section, compute $H^k(C_n,\mathbb{Z})$ and $H_k(C_n,\mathbb{Z})$ for trivial action, and check $H_1(C_n,\mathbb{Z})\cong C_n^{\mathrm{ab}}$.
blocks.solution:
Apply $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ to $\cdots\xrightarrow{N}\mathbb{Z}G\xrightarrow{t-1}\mathbb{Z}G\xrightarrow{N}\mathbb{Z}G\xrightarrow{t-1}\mathbb{Z}G$. Each $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}G}(\mathbb{Z}G,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ (a map is determined by the image of $1$), $t-1$ induces multiplication by $1-1 = 0$ and $N$ induces multiplication by $n$. The cochain complex is
$$\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\cdots$$
in degrees $0,1,2,3,\dots$. Hence $H^0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H^{\mathrm{odd}} = \ker(n)/0 = 0$, and $H^{2k} = \mathbb{Z}/n$ for $k\ge1$.

For homology apply $\mathbb{Z}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}G}-$; again each term becomes $\mathbb{Z}$ with $t-1\mapsto0$, $N\mapsto n$, giving $\cdots\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $\dots,3,2,1,0$. So $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_{\mathrm{odd}} = \mathbb{Z}/n$, $H_{2k} = 0$ for $k\ge1$. In particular $H_1(C_n,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}/n = C_n^{\mathrm{ab}}$, as Arapura's Theorem 5.31 predicts. Also $H^2(C_n,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$ classifies the extensions $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to E\to C_n\to1$ (all central, since the action is trivial). Two of them are visible at once: the split one, $E = \mathbb{Z}\times C_n$, and $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to C_n\to0$, which does not split because $\mathbb{Z}$ has no element of order $n$.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $H^k(C_n,\mathbb{Z}/n)$ and $H^k(C_2,\mathbb{Z}_-)$, where $\mathbb{Z}_-$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ with the generator acting by $-1$.
2. Show $H_1(G,\mathbb{Z})\cong G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ for any group $G$ by applying $\mathbb{Z}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}G}-$ to $0\to I\to\mathbb{Z}G\to\mathbb{Z}\to0$, where $I$ is the augmentation ideal, and using $I/I^2\cong G^{\mathrm{ab}}$.

blocks.title: Derived limits
blocks.body:
The inverse limit of a tower $A_0\xleftarrow{f_1}A_1\xleftarrow{f_2}A_2\leftarrow\cdots$ of abelian groups is the kernel of
$$\Delta\colon\prod_iA_i\to\prod_iA_i,\qquad\Delta(a_i)_i = \big(a_i-f_{i+1}(a_{i+1})\big)_i,$$
and Weibel defines $\lim^1A_i = \operatorname{coker}\Delta$ (Definition 3.5.1). The functor $\lim$ is left exact but not exact, and $\lim^1$ measures the failure; Weibel sets $\lim^n = 0$ for $n\ge2$ on towers and shows that $\lim,\lim^1$ form a $\delta$-functor (Lemma 3.5.2) and that on towers they are the right derived functors of $\lim$ (Corollary 3.5.4). For inverse systems indexed by larger posets (Bannister works over $\omega^\kappa$), the higher derived functors $\lim^n$ need not vanish; Bannister's paper studies exactly these higher derived limits, computes them through an explicit alternating cochain complex whose $n$-th cohomology is $\lim^n$ (his Definition 3.5 and Proposition 3.7), and draws consequences for strong homology.

blocks.title: The lim-lim^1 sequence
blocks.body:
Let $0\to(A_i)\to(B_i)\to(C_i)\to0$ be a short exact sequence of towers (exact at each $i$, with compatible maps). Then there is an exact sequence
$$0\to\lim A_i\to\lim B_i\to\lim C_i\to\lim{}^1A_i\to\lim{}^1B_i\to\lim{}^1C_i\to0.$$
If all maps $f_i$ of a tower are surjective, its $\lim^1$ is zero (Weibel Lemma 3.5.3); more generally $\lim^1 = 0$ for towers satisfying the Mittag-Leffler condition, that the images of $A_{i+k}\to A_i$ stabilise for each $i$ (Weibel Proposition 3.5.7, not proved here).

Products of short exact sequences of abelian groups are exact, so $0\to\prod A_i\to\prod B_i\to\prod C_i\to0$ is exact, and $\Delta$ acts compatibly on the three products. The snake lemma applied to $\Delta$ gives exactly the six-term sequence, since $\lim = \ker\Delta$ and $\lim^1 = \operatorname{coker}\Delta$; the outer zeros come from the injectivity and surjectivity addenda of the snake lemma.

If every $f_i$ is surjective and $(b_i)\in\prod A_i$, solve $a_i-f_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = b_i$ recursively: put $a_0 = 0$, and having $a_i$ choose $a_{i+1}$ with $f_{i+1}(a_{i+1}) = a_i-b_i$. Then $\Delta(a) = b$, so $\Delta$ is onto.

blocks.title: A non-zero lim^1
blocks.body: Compute $\lim$ and $\lim^1$ of the tower $\mathbb{Z}\xleftarrow{p}\mathbb{Z}\xleftarrow{p}\mathbb{Z}\leftarrow\cdots$.
blocks.solution:
The tower is isomorphic to the tower of subgroups $\mathbb{Z}\supseteq p\mathbb{Z}\supseteq p^2\mathbb{Z}\supseteq\cdots$ with inclusions ($p^i\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}$ via division by $p^i$). Consider the short exact sequence of towers
$$0\to(p^i\mathbb{Z})_i\to(\mathbb{Z})_i\to(\mathbb{Z}/p^i)_i\to0,$$
where the middle tower is constant with identity maps and the right-hand one has the reduction maps. The constant tower has $\lim = \mathbb{Z}$ and $\lim^1 = 0$ (its maps are onto); the tower $\mathbb{Z}/p^i$ has surjective maps, so $\lim^1 = 0$, and $\lim = \mathbb{Z}_p$, the $p$-adic integers; and $\lim p^i\mathbb{Z} = \bigcap_ip^i\mathbb{Z} = 0$. The six-term sequence becomes
$$0\to0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}_p\to\lim{}^1(p^i\mathbb{Z})\to0\to0\to0,$$
so $\lim^1 = \mathbb{Z}_p/\mathbb{Z}$, an uncountable group, although every group in the tower is $\mathbb{Z}$. In topology this is why the Milnor sequence $0\to\lim^1H^{q-1}(X_i)\to H^q(X)\to\lim H^q(X_i)\to0$ for an increasing union of subcomplexes (Weibel Application 3.5.9) can have a large correction term.

blocks.title: Beyond modules: Grothendieck's axioms, derived and exact categories
blocks.body:
Three generalisations appear in the papers, and the page now has the vocabulary to state them.

1. Grothendieck's axioms. In an abelian category, AB3 asks that all coproducts exist, AB4 that coproducts of short exact sequences are exact, and AB5 that filtered colimits are exact; AB3* and AB4* are the dual conditions for products. Modules satisfy AB5 and AB4*, but not AB5*: inverse limits are not exact, and the failure is exactly $\lim^1$. Tang's paper checks which axioms hold for profinite and solid modules (its Sections 1-2), because derived functors and the comparison of Ext groups depend on them. The Stacks Project discusses the relevant property for products in its Section 12.32.
2. Derived categories. The derived category $D(\mathcal{A})$ has complexes as objects and inverts quasi-isomorphisms. Then $\mathrm{Ext}^i(X,Y) = \mathrm{Hom}_{D(\mathcal{A})}(X,Y[i])$ for all complexes, the long exact Ext sequences come from distinguished triangles, and Yoneda Ext and derived Ext are identified (Stacks Section 13.27). Tang defers this to his Section 4. This page only uses the phrase; the subject belongs to a later page.
3. Exact categories and relative homological algebra. In Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson's formulation (their Definition 3.2, equivalent to Quillen's axioms), an exact structure on an abelian category is a class $\mathcal{E}$ of short exact sequences, the 'admissible' ones, closed under isomorphism, such that identities are admissible monos and epis, admissible monos and admissible epis are closed under composition, admissible monos are stable under pushout along any map, and admissible epis are stable under pullback along any map. The split sequences form the smallest exact structure and all short exact sequences the largest. On a general additive category one asks the same of a class of kernel-cokernel pairs. Restricting to a smaller class of short exact sequences on a module category gives relative projectives (objects $P$ with $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ exact on admissible sequences) and a relative $\mathrm{Ext}^1$, the classes of admissible extensions inside $\mathrm{Ext}^1$; the paper's Remark 3.6 describes an exact structure as a closed additive subbifunctor of $\mathrm{Ext}^1(-,-)$, so these classes form a subgroup under Baer sum. This is the framework of Blanchette-Brüstle-Hanson, who choose exact structures on persistence modules so that minimal relative projective resolutions give homological invariants such as relative Betti numbers and the rank invariant. Their Grothendieck groups and Krull-Remak-Schmidt decompositions are not covered here.

1. Show that in the category of abelian groups, a product of short exact sequences is exact (AB4*), but that the inverse limit of the short exact sequences $0\to p^i\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/p^i\to0$ is not exact.
2. Show that the split short exact sequences form an exact structure on any additive category, and that every object is relatively projective for it.
3. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the class of short exact sequences of abelian groups on which every functor $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/m,-)$ is exact. Show that each $\mathbb{Z}/m$ is relatively projective for $\mathcal{E}$, that $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\to0$ is not in $\mathcal{E}$, and that the classes in $\mathrm{Ext}^1(C,A)$ of sequences in $\mathcal{E}$ form a subgroup.

blocks.title: Reading the papers
blocks.body:
Here is where each paper's homological prerequisites are treated on this page.

1. Holanda and Miranda-Neto, Cohen-Macaulay Burch rings. Ext and Tor of finitely generated modules over a Noetherian local ring (sections on Tor and Ext), vanishing criteria for freeness (Ext detects projectives; minimal resolutions over local rings), projective and injective dimension (homological dimension), Hom-tensor adjunction and dualities of the form $\mathrm{Tor}^\vee\cong\mathrm{Ext}(-,(-)^\vee)$ (more tools for Ext), double complexes and the two spectral sequences (balancing; spectral sequences proper are on the [[spectral-sequences]] page). Depth, its description by $\mathrm{Ext}^i(k,-)$, the depth lemma and the Auslander-Buchsbaum formula, with the definition of maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules (depth and Auslander-Buchsbaum). Not here: canonical modules, local duality, and the vanishing of $\mathrm{Ext}^{q}(N,\omega_R)$ for $q>0$ and maximal Cohen-Macaulay $N$, which the proof of their Theorem 2.1 quotes from the literature.
2. Blanchette, Brüstle and Hanson, exact structures for persistence modules. Abelian categories and exact functors (first sections), projectives and their characterisation by $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ (views on projectives), global dimension (homological dimension), extensions, pullbacks, pushouts and Baer sum (extensions and Yoneda Ext), exact structures and relative Ext (beyond modules). Not here: almost split sequences, representation dimension, Grothendieck groups.
3. Tang, profinite and solid cohomology. Grothendieck's AB axioms (beyond modules), enough projectives (enough projectives and injectives), Ext as derived functor and as Yoneda Ext and their agreement (extensions and Yoneda Ext), computing Ext from a projective resolution (Ext), group cohomology as Ext over a group ring (group cohomology). Not here: condensed and solid mathematics.
4. Bannister, derived limits in the Cohen model. Inverse systems, left exactness of $\lim$, $\lim^n$ as derived functors (derived limits), the snake lemma long exact sequence (snake lemma; lim-lim^1 sequence), injectives, divisible groups and right adjoints of exact functors (Baer's criterion; enough injectives), acyclicity and uniqueness of universal $\delta$-functors (derived functors and delta-functors). Not here: the set theory.
5. Debray et al., the Smith fiber sequence. Long exact sequences as computational tools, the five lemma (used in its Section 5.1 to see that a map of long exact sequences is an isomorphism), extension problems (snake and five lemma; extension problems), and the short exact sequence $0\to\mathrm{Ext}^1(\pi_{m-1}X,\mathbb{Z})\to[X,\Sigma^mI_{\mathbb{Z}}]\to\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_mX,\mathbb{Z})\to0$ behind Anderson duality, with the reason a long exact sequence cannot be dualised by $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb{Z})$ termwise (Ext into the integers and Anderson duality). Not here: spectra, bordism and Thom spectra themselves, which the reader must take from the paper's Section 2.

- $\mathrm{Ext}^1(A,B)$ counts equivalence classes of extensions, not isomorphism types of the middle module. There are $p$ extensions of $\mathbb{Z}/p$ by $\mathbb{Z}/p$ but only two possible middle groups.
- The universal coefficient sequences split, but not naturally. One may not use the splitting to define maps between cohomology groups of different spaces.
- Ext and Tor depend on the ring: $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}/2}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = 0$, and over $\mathbb{Z}/4$ every $\mathrm{Ext}^n$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Always record the subscript.
- Ext is a right derived functor (Hom is left exact); Tor is a left derived functor ($\otimes$ is right exact). At least one expository source in the dossier, an REU paper, calls Ext 'left-derived'; that is a slip.
- The symmetry $\mathrm{Tor}_n(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n(B,A)$ is not formal. It needs the balancing theorem, and Arapura remarks that the argument in one standard textbook is incomplete and points to Weibel's Theorem 2.7.2 instead. For non-commutative $R$ the correct statement is $\mathrm{Tor}^R_n(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}^{R^{op}}_n(B,A)$.

- Projective implies flat for modules, but Tang points out that this can fail in non-classical settings such as solid modules, where Tor must then be computed by resolving both variables.
- Derived-functor Ext needs enough projectives or enough injectives. Without them, use Yoneda Ext or the derived category; with them, all three agree.
- Localisation commutes with Ext for finitely generated first arguments over Noetherian rings (Weibel 3.3.10), but not in general; $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Z}) = 0$ while its 'localisation' at $0$ would be $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q})\ne0$.
- Flat is weaker than projective: $\mathbb{Q}$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$ but not projective. Finitely presented flat modules are projective (Weibel Theorem 3.2.7).
- 'Higher Ext is just diagram chasing' is a common first impression, as the r/math thread shows. The answers there point to Yoneda's $n$-extensions and to the homotopical reading; the conceptual content is that the groups do not depend on the resolution, which is why they can be computed in whichever way is convenient.

This page is the foundation of several later ones. [[cohomology]] of spaces uses the universal coefficient theorem and the long exact sequences built here. [[spectral-sequences]] start from the double complexes of the balancing section and organise iterated long exact sequences. [[sheaf-cohomology]] is the right derived functor of global sections, computed by injective or acyclic resolutions, exactly as in the derived functor section. [[galois-cohomology]] is group cohomology $\mathrm{Ext}^n_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z},M)$ for profinite Galois groups, with continuity built in, which is where Tang's paper begins. In commutative algebra, [[localization]] is the basic example of a flat base change, and finitely generated modules over [[noetherian-rings]] have resolutions by finitely generated free modules. The adjunctions used throughout (Hom-tensor, coinduction) are instances of [[yoneda-adjunctions]].

1. Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ be an exact sequence of finite abelian groups. Using the long exact Ext sequence with $M = \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$, show that $0\to C^*\to B^*\to A^*\to0$ is exact.
2. Let $R$ be commutative Noetherian local with residue field $k$, and $M$ finitely generated. Show that $M$ is free if and only if $\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(M,k) = 0$.
3. Show that $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}}(A,\mathbb{Z}) = 0$ for a finitely generated $A$ if and only if $A$ is free. Is the finite generation hypothesis used in both directions?
4. Let $R = \mathbb{Z}[x]$. Compute $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(R/(2,x),R/(2,x))$ for all $i$ using a Koszul resolution, and $\mathrm{pd}_R\,R/(2,x)$.
5. Compute $H^n(C_2\times C_2,\mathbb{Z}/2)$ for $n\le2$ from a free resolution of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{F}_2[C_2\times C_2]\cong\mathbb{F}_2[x,y]/(x^2,y^2)$.
